text:
# Chapter 1: The Address That Hummed

In the city of Oru, no one gave directions by pointing. A finger could indicate a wall, but a wall might be elsewhere by supper. People navigated by listening for the rooms they wanted. A kitchen with a remembered argument clicked its pipes. A nursery hummed a lullaby even after its children had grown old. The Registry called these sounds addresses. Everyone else called them manners.

Ivara Noll worked in the Vellum Hall, where addresses were copied onto strips of skin-thin bark and pinned to a map that had no north. Her desk stood beside the Mouth Room, a chamber inside the Hall where new rooms were asked to say what they were. Its door was a circular slab of black wood with a brass lip. When it opened, the room inside gave a note like a spoon touching a cup.

“Not a room,” said Tovan Sere, listening with his left ear. He was the Hall's senior examiner, though the younger clerks called him the Chair because he never stood while deciding anything. “A pocket. A room has a door that expects to be used.”

Ivara wrote pocket on the Mouth Room's bark strip. The word made the Mouth Room's note flatten. She scratched it out.

At her elbow sat a red key, a long iron thing with a forked tooth. Her mother had left it with no label and no lock to fit. Ivara kept it because it warmed when she lied. She had tested this carefully, first telling it that she liked turnip broth, then that she had never entered the Understair. It warmed at the second claim. The Understair was a maintenance passage below Vellum Hall, officially sealed since Ivara was small.

Across the aisle, Eren Vey sorted address strips by the pressure of their sound. He was a careful young clerk whose voice went thin at the end of every sentence, as if the rest of him had stepped through a door. Three desks away, Eren Vell, a porter with the same narrow face and almost the same name, carried stacks of bark to the drying racks. The two Eren’s had learned to answer only to their surnames. When someone called “Eren,” both looked up and Tovan deducted a minute of their pay.

The city had sent a petition that morning: a room was missing from the Tin Orchard. The Orchard was not a garden, though it contained rust-colored trees. Each tree grew a hollow metal fruit in which a family could keep a private address. Somewhere among the trees was a little room called the Latch, where the Orchard's caretaker stored spare door hinges. The petition said the Latch had vanished without taking its hinge inventory with it. That was impossible. Rooms did not leave their contents behind.

“Who signed?” asked Tovan.

“A name, Lio,” said Ivara. “I took it for a woman’s name. It says she is the last person who remembers the door.”

“Then we have two problems,” said the Chair. “The room and the memory.”

Tovan sent Ivara and Eren Vey to inspect the Orchard. Before she left, Ivara slid the red key into her cuff. Eren Vell stopped at the Hall's outer door to hand her a parcel tied with blue thread. “For the Orchard keeper,” he said. “A tin box from the lost-property shelf. Don't open it. It has been waiting longer than I have.”

The tin box was warm, too. Ivara put the tin box in her satchel and kept the key in her cuff. She did not ask why the parcel had no label. In the Registry, a question without an address could wander for days.

The Tin Orchard rang in the afternoon, each metal fruit making a different note as the branches shifted. The trees grew in shallow trays of pale grit. Their roots were loops of wire, and their leaves were tiny hinged tags that clicked together like teeth. Nima Orrel, the Orchard keeper, came to meet them. She wore a necklace of brass washers, one for each year she had lived in the Orchard.

“Lio isn't a person,” Nima said. “It's what the missing room calls itself when it wants to be found.” Ivara understood that the petition had mistaken a room's name for its signer.

Ivara glanced at Eren. “You signed the petition.”

“I signed the petition that arrived,” said Nima. “The ink was already there.”

She led them to a tray with an empty ring of grit. A single hinge lay in the center. Its pin bore a faded blue stain. Ivara thought of Eren Vell's parcel, still in her bag.

“Who was here last?” asked Eren Vey.

“I was,” Nima said. “I put the hinge down. I heard the Latch ask me to keep quiet. Then the path ended.”

The false certainty in her voice came from practice. Nima believed the Latch had been built by Nima's grandmother, and that her grandmother had hidden it to protect the Orchard. Everyone in Oru knew the tale: the old woman, the hinge, the room that slipped away. Ivara had copied the official version herself.

But there was no sound in the empty ring. A vanished room should leave an echo. Ivara crouched and heard instead a faint tapping from inside the grit. She took out the red key. Its prongs trembled toward the ground.

“That key is not on the inventory,” Nima said.

“Neither is this room,” said Ivara.

She turned the key in the grit. A narrow seam opened, no wider than a thread, and from below came a voice that sounded exactly like the Mouth Room's note. The Orchard had a floor under its floor.

Eren Vey caught her sleeve before she could put her fingers into the seam. “We should record this first.”

“If we record it, the Hall will close it.”

“If we don't, the room can move.”

Ivara looked at the empty hinge ring, the blue thread, and the parcel in her satchel. She knew, then, that Eren Vell had sent her the box for a reason. She did not yet know what he had put inside.

Nima set her palm over the seam. “My grandmother made the Latch,” she said. “It belongs to our family.”

The red key stayed cool in Ivara's hand. Nima believed the inherited story, though the story was wrong.

That night, Ivara did not go home. The Hall's sleeping gallery held thirty narrow bunks, each with a tag that named its occupant and one room they were permitted to dream in. Her tag said “Ivara Noll: Vellum Hall.” She turned it over. On the back, someone had written Alis Noll in faded red ink.

The letters reminded Ivara of her mother's old recipe sheets, but the hand was not Mara's. Mara Noll wrote every letter with a small gap in its middle, as though each word had a door in it. Ivara went to her desk and searched the drawers for the sheet where Mara had recorded a recipe for shell milk. She did not find it. The name on the back of her sleeping tag had not come from this page. The letters had faded, but the writing itself was recent; someone had added the name since Mara's last recipe sheet.

She found Eren Vey still at his desk. “Did you put this on my tag?”

He inspected it without touching. “No. The tag is telling you where it thinks you belong.”

“Tags don't think.”

“They don't have to. They only need a little pressure from the room.”

He explained that the first Hall clerks had not pinned addresses to a map. They pinned them to people. When a room moved, the people who had used it carried its location in their habits: how they paused at a turn, what they called a threshold, which side of a cup they reached for. Later clerks replaced these living records with tags and maps. Eren believed the Hall still listened to people, even when it pretended to listen only to paper.

“Why did you come here?” Ivara asked.

“My mother said I was born in the wrong room.” He tapped his own tag. It held no birthplace. “I want to know what she meant.”

The question made Ivara think of the report from the Orchard. Nima had signed it without remembering signing. The name Lio had appeared without a hand to write it. Perhaps a room could use a person's habits, too, and borrow a name when it had no other way to knock.

Eren showed her a thin scar across his wrist. A door had closed on it when he was very young, he said, but the door had been in a wall that no longer existed. He had never told the Registry. “If a room can keep part of you, then maybe it can keep a person.”

Ivara touched the red key through her cuff. It was cold. She hadn't lied, but she had kept a thought to herself: she sometimes heard a quiet second note under the Mouth Room's tone. Now it came again, so soft she could have blamed the pipes.

At dawn, the Hall called all clerks to the map. A new strip of bark had appeared by the Orchard's address. It bore no words, only a pair of small handprints. The younger clerks laughed and said a child had touched the wet bark. Tovan said nothing. He turned the strip face down and ordered Ivara to leave it alone.

She turned it face up again once the Chair had gone. The handprints were the exact size of her own hands before she could speak.

At the end of the morning shift, Ivara took the handprint strip to Tovan. He studied it for a long while, then brought out a ledger with a cracked spine. The book recorded the Hall's repairs, with a few private notes Tovan had added about residents. On the first page, in the same red ink, was a list of places that had been joined and separated. Beside each place was the name of the clerk who authorized the work.

Mara Noll appeared beside the first division. Tovan's name appeared beside the second. Ivara asked what the marks meant. He told her that Mara had argued against dividing the first house, but eventually signed the order to protect the children inside. He had signed the follow-up that made the division permanent.

“Did she tell you what happened to Alis?”

“She asked me to keep the address quiet.”

“That's not the same thing.”

“No,” Tovan said. “It isn't.”

He shut the ledger before she could read the other names. Ivara noticed a mark beside Eren Vey's birthplace, an open door drawn in blue. Tovan saw her notice it and did not cover the mark. That, more than his answer, told her that he had begun to understand what he owed them.

She left the Hall with the handprint strip tucked into her coat. Outside, the city had no streets in the usual sense. There were lanes made by repeated journeys, and the lanes grew firmer whenever enough people traveled them for the same reason. The path to the Orchard had become a shallow groove in the stone. Ivara followed it, listening to its small echo beneath her shoes.

At the gate, Nima's necklace made a distant chime. The Orchard keeper had begun the evening count, one washer for each tree that had offered its fruit to a family. The necklace counted Nima's years; this was a separate count. Ivara understood now why the trees were called an orchard even though they grew no food. Each one held a memory with a hard shell around it. The fruit could be opened only by the person who had put the address inside.

Somewhere under the grit, the missing room tapped once. Ivara pressed the handprint strip to the ground. For a breath, she felt a child's fingers push back from the other side.

# Chapter 2: The Box With No Bottom

After the Orchard closed its gates, Ivara returned to the Vellum Hall alone. Eren Vey was waiting there. The tin box knocked against Ivara's hip as she walked. It was lighter than a box should be, and the tapping from within followed the rhythm of her steps, half a beat late.

Tovan had locked the Mouth Room. He stood outside it with a bone comb in his hand. Its teeth were different lengths, and each tooth bore a tiny number. The comb had belonged to an earlier keeper of the Hall, who used it to comb the sounds from a new room until it could speak plainly. Tovan claimed he had borrowed it from the Hall's collection of unwanted instruments. The collection denied owning it. Under Ivara's cuff, the red key warmed; Tovan had not borrowed it.

“You brought back an unregistered seam,” he said. “And a sound that matches this room.”

“Did the Mouth Room move?” asked Ivara.

“No. It answered from the Orchard.”

Eren Vey set his notes on the table. “A room can share a voice.”

“People share a voice. Rooms share walls.” Tovan turned the comb over. “Unless they're the same room.”

At that, Ivara felt the red key stay cool in her cuff; Tovan's suggestion was true. She removed the tin box and put it on the table. The parcel's blue thread had gone slack. A small folded paper lay beneath the false bottom, tucked beside the map and thimble, though she had not opened the box.

Tovan read the note aloud: “A room may be stored by its first name, but not its walls.” The note was signed E. Vell.

“You gave this to me,” Ivara said.

“I gave you a box,” said Eren Vell from the doorway. “I didn't know there was a note.” The porter had come in without his usual stack of bark. His palms were stained with blue ink.

The two Erens stood facing each other. Eren Vey looked down at the note. “You wrote that.”

Eren Vell laughed, which made his face look less like the clerk's. “I don't write. I carry.”

The claim seemed true until Ivara saw the ink on his palms. The red key warmed: Pell was lying. Ivara picked up the box. Its inside was lined with felt, but when she tilted it, the tapping came from somewhere deeper than the base.

Tovan demanded the parcel. Ivara refused. She took the box to the Understair, with Eren Vey behind her and Eren Vell ahead. The passage was still officially sealed, though its door had been painted over and the paint had a fresh crack running through the middle. Under the stairs, the air smelled of wet paper though there was no water in Oru.

The passage narrowed into a room called the Sump, where discarded addresses were pressed into clay. In its center stood a stone basin. Ivara set the tin box inside it. The box lifted its lid by itself. A little brass map lay within, folded into a square. On its face, the map showed the Tin Orchard, the Vellum Hall, and a narrow room drawn between them. That room had no entrance. In its center was the word LATCH.

Beneath the map, they found a glass thimble containing a black thread. The thimble was capped with red wax. The tin box had looked empty because its bottom was hinged upward; the objects had been tucked in the false base.

Eren Vey leaned close. “The plan on this map is older than the Orchard,” Eren Vey said.

“Older than the Hall,” said Eren Vell. “The brass copy is newer. It shows rooms before they were divided.”

Tovan arrived carrying the bone comb. He had taken the other staircase, or perhaps the Sump had brought him to them. The passage did not always preserve the route a person used. He ran the comb over the map. Each remaining numbered tooth vibrated. At the empty seventh place, the map shivered and the drawn Latch turned sideways.

Ivara understood that Tovan had lied about borrowing the comb: it had not come from the collection. It had been waiting for this map. “What is the black thread?”

“An address before it learned to make a sound,” Tovan said. “If someone pulls it, the room may come back.”

“Or the room may unravel,” said Eren Vey.

Tovan looked at the two men. “You both know more than you say.”

text:
Eren Vell took the thimble from the box. “I used to be called Pell Aven. The Hall erased my name when the Latch disappeared. I was its child.”

The name landed with a sound like a lock finding its slot. Ivara had heard the name Pell Aven in an old file: an apprentice missing from the Registry's winter roll. The porter was the same person, and he had carried the name Eren Vell for eight years. The Hall had not forgotten him; it had filed him under a job instead of a life.

Eren Vey stepped back from him. “You were the apprentice who stole the seventh tooth.”

“I found it in the false bottom,” Pell said. “Tovan had hidden it there. Before I sent you the box, I moved the tooth beneath the moth in the hidden chamber. The comb was breaking rooms into pieces, and I thought the Latch could keep them together.”

The truth explained the missing tooth and the false bottom. It did not explain the blue thread, or why the Latch had called to Ivara. She had never met Pell before he became Eren Vell. At least, that was what she believed.

The red key stayed cool. Tovan snatched the map from the basin, but the line between Hall and Orchard remained in the stone beneath it. A new door appeared in the Sump wall, small and round, with a brass lip.

From behind it, someone tapped three times.

Ivara put the glass thimble in her pocket. Pell kept the tin box. Eren Vey held the map, and Tovan held the bone comb. Four people, four objects, and an unopened door that knew the Mouth Room's note.

They did not open the round door. Tovan insisted that a door must be named before it was entered, but the small tapping continued from the other side. The sound was not impatient. It was counting their breaths.

Eren Vey asked Pell how he had come by the box. Pell said it had been on the lost-property shelf when he began work at the Hall, and that he had avoided it for years. On the day it was placed in Ivara's hands, it had appeared beside his porter cart. There was no record of a delivery. He had tied blue thread around it because the box's lid would not stay shut.

“Did you know what was inside?” Ivara asked.

“No. I knew who it was meant for.”

“Who?”

Pell looked at the crack in the door. “Someone who hears the note without asking what it means.”

Ivara could not tell whether he meant herself or the room. She took out the red key and laid it on the stone basin. The key did not warm or cool. Tovan said that was not an answer. Eren Vey replied that silence was often the only answer a room could give without being claimed.

The brass map showed no route from the Sump to the round door. Tovan reached for the map, then stopped. Eren turned it upside down. A cluster of marks appeared, all on the side where the false bottom had pressed against the paper. The marks formed a row of five seats, just as if the map were a place setting. He recognized the number because he had found five names in the hidden chamber once, in a childhood dream he thought was invented.

Pell watched him. “You remember the house?”

“I remember a song, but not the place.”

“Whose song?”

“I don't know.”

The black thread in the thimble quivered. Eren pulled his hand away. He said that the song had followed him to the Hall, but he had never heard it when anyone else was present. He had decided it was his mother's humming, though he had no proof. Now, in the Sump, the thread repeated the same three notes.

Tovan sat on the basin's rim. For the first time that day, he looked old. He told them the Registry was founded after a terrible confusion called the Great Partition, when rooms had been joined and divided without consent. The Hall's first examiners made the comb to separate each room's voice. The comb was a safeguard. It was also the instrument that caused the division.

“Which is why you kept the seventh tooth,” Ivara said.

“I did not keep it. I hid it where no one would use it.”

“Those are the same thing, if you have the only map.”

text:
Tovan accepted that. He turned the bone comb over in his hands, and the numbered teeth made a faint dry chatter. The missing seventh tooth had been designed to listen for a room's first name, before it acquired all the names people later gave it. That was why it could both mend and undo the comb's work. The red key in Ivara's hand was a separate object: iron, forked, and warm with a lie. It was not a tooth from the bone comb.

Ivara looked again at the brass map. The line to the Latch did not lead down. It led through the Hall, past the Mouth Room, to the handprints on the new bark strip. She had seen the marks that morning, disobeyed Tovan, and turned the strip face up again. She realized the Hall had begun answering her, not the Registry.

The three taps came again, now from the inside of the box. Pell placed it on the floor. The lid lifted and settled three times. On the fourth, it stayed open. A second note, lower than the first, sounded from the round door. It was the answer to the Mouth Room's tone.

They moved away from the basin toward the surface passage, but remained in the Sump. Ivara tried to take the brass map, but it clung to the basin as if the stone had grown around its edges. Eren Vey said the map might be choosing its first bearer. He laid his palm beside it and described the childhood song he had heard. The map released with a soft click.

Pell watched him take it. “Does it feel familiar?”

“It feels like someone has remembered me.”

That was different from being recognized by the Hall. Eren put the map inside his coat. The glass thimble remained with Ivara, and the bone comb with Tovan. The box, still open, looked smaller now that the things hidden inside had been found.

Tovan asked Pell to describe the day the seventh tooth disappeared. Pell remembered the comb lying on the table in the first house. The children had been told not to touch it because the sound of the teeth could change a room. He had not understood the warning. Tovan had hidden the seventh tooth in the false bottom. Pell found it there, then moved it beneath the moth and tied it to the spool, hoping the comb would stop dividing the house. The comb did stop, but the room's names had already begun to separate.

“Why didn't you tell us?” Ivara asked.

“I tried to tell the Hall. The name I used was Pell Aven. Nobody found it in the files. When I told them I knew where the tooth was, they searched for a porter named Pell and found no one. Eventually I became the person they expected to see.”

The Hall had not literally changed his face. It had narrowed the ways he could introduce himself until one name was easier than all the others. Ivara could see how a mistaken record became a habit, and a habit became a life.

The round door tapped a fourth time. This time, the bone comb answered without Tovan touching it. Its unnumbered gap gave off a faint shimmer. He held the comb away from the box. The whole Sump floor tilted by a degree, and the clay addresses slid toward the stone basin.

Eren Vey caught the map before it fell. Its folded edges opened against his chest. Every line led to the chamber in the wall. Pell recognized the shape as the plan of the house before the division: one room with five thresholds, each threshold opening wherever a person needed to enter.

“Not a door,” said Tovan. “A choice.”

The distinction stayed with Ivara. She looked at the round outline and waited. The tapping stopped. Nobody had opened it, and still the room had let them hear its answer. They were learning to approach without forcing an entrance.

# Chapter 3: The Passenger in the Wall

The three taps came again. Ivara took the red key from the stone basin, then answered with two, though nobody had taught her the pattern. A seam opened around the round door. Beyond it lay a strip of darkness so narrow that a person could pass only sideways.

Tovan lifted the bone comb. “We should take this to the Hall and make a proper record.”

“Then it will be classified as a pocket,” said Ivara, “and forgotten with the other pockets.”

The room behind the door tapped once. Pell held the tin box against his chest. “I know that sound.”

He went through first. On the other side, the narrow passage beyond the round door widened into a little chamber lined with paper. Every wall was covered by names in different hands. The names had been crossed out so many times that some were only grooves. At the center sat a child-sized chair, and on the chair lay a chalk moth. It was flat and white, with two wings shaped like spoons.

“I left that,” Pell said. “I was small.”

Ivara looked at him. “Eren Vey said he remembered the song, but not the place.”

“That was Eren Vey. I said I didn't remember the place.”

There was a difference, and the red key stayed cool. Pell had told the truth, though not the whole truth.

Eren Vey turned the brass map toward the chalk moth. The line between the Hall and the Orchard moved beneath his thumb. A new line appeared, tracing the narrow chamber and then continuing through the wall. “This is not a map of places,” he said. “It's a map of who can remember them.”

The names on the wall were those of children born in rooms that had gone missing. Some had become clerks, some porters, some simply disappeared from the census. Ivara found her own name cut into the paper, though she had no memory of entering the chamber. Beside it was a second name: Alis Noll.

The old ledger said Alis had been buried in the family niche. The Hall's register listed her as “unplaced at birth.” Ivara had assumed the phrase meant her sister had not taken a first breath.

The chalk moth lifted one wing. Beneath it lay a numbered spool, the seventh tooth from the comb tied around its middle. Tovan lunged. Ivara caught his wrist.

“You knew Alis,” she said.

“I knew her file,” he answered.

The red key warmed. This was another practiced answer. Tovan had known the child.

He took the key from Ivara and pressed it to the chalk moth. The flat creature opened its wings. A small voice came out of it, the note from the Mouth Room, followed by a girl's whisper: “Don't let them divide the first house.”

Tovan went pale. Eren Vey stared at him. Ivara turned to Tovan. “Who was Alis to me?”

“Alis,” Tovan said. “She was not your sister by blood. She was your sister by address. Mara brought her home through the Mouth Room and into the Latch.”

The correction struck like a dropped stone. Ivara had believed Alis dead and buried. She had not been buried. Tovan had helped hide her in the first house, before rooms had separate names. The Partition divided the first house into the Vellum Hall and the Tin Orchard so each could be governed. Its hidden rooms endured between them. When the division began to fail, it cut the names of every person born between the parts.

Pell had been a child in that dividing house. He remembered Alis as a friend, and the wall remembered them both. He touched the paper beside her name. The grooves filled with ink, letter by letter.

Tovan gave Ivara back the red key. “Your mother asked me to keep the girl hidden. She said the Latch would be safest if no one could find it.”

“Then why did you say it was sealed?”

“Because it was. I believed the Latch could not open again.”

That belief had lasted for years. It fell now, though Tovan kept his eyes on the wall.

text:
The numbered spool rolled from beneath the moth and stopped at Eren Vey's boot. He picked it up, unwound a short length, and listened. He heard a name nobody else could hear. He did not tell them what it was. Instead, he put the spool in his coat and said, “We need to go to the Nacre Stair.”

Ivara asked why.

“Because someone is pulling the other end.”

They left the chamber. When they turned back, the round door had become an unmarked panel. Pell carried the tin box, Ivara the thimble, Tovan the comb, Eren the map and spool. The chalk moth remained in the chair.

At the Understair threshold, Pell stopped and told Ivara that he had sent the box because her mother once said Ivara could hear a room without trying to own it. He had not known whether she would come.

The red key stayed cool in Ivara's palm. She believed him.

They studied the paper wall until the lamps in the passage began to dim. Each crossed-out name carried a small mark beside it: a circle for a room that had been joined, a square for a room that had been divided, and a line for a person who had moved away. Beside Alis's name was a small open door. Beside Ivara's was a key.

“Who wrote these?” asked Eren Vey.

“Children,” Pell said. “We marked the wall so it would remember what the grownups wanted to split.”

Pell told them he had arrived at the first house as a boy whose name could not stay in one place. One week the Orchard called him Pell; the Hall called him Aven; the stair did not call him anything. His mother brought him there because the house could hold all of him at once. He had played with Alis and Nima, and the baby Ivara had slept in a drawer padded with old bark.

“I knew the Hall had made you a porter. I didn't know you had been Pell Aven before that,” Ivara said.

“I thought that was what I was allowed to be.”

Eren Vey turned to the wall and found his own name. It had not been crossed out. The open door beside it pointed toward the Hall. He had spent a single night in the first house when he was very young, but he had not been one of the four children who named it. The room had remembered him anyway. He saw now that the note in his voice was the same note that called from the Mouth Room.

Ivara asked Tovan how he had known her mother. He said Mara Noll had worked as a clerk at the Hall before Ivara was born. She had cared for Alis before and after the Partition, and she had taken the red key when the first house became inaccessible. Mara had not been the girl's birth mother, but she had been the person who taught both sisters to call a room home.

“You made me think she was dead,” Ivara said.

“I made you think she was buried. I knew she was alive, but I did not know whether the room could keep her safe.”

The key stayed cool. This time Tovan had told the truth about what he knew; Ivara still had reason to resent his choice. The Registry treated such corrections as harmless errors. The people inside the errors had to live with them.

The chalk moth's wings opened wider. It spoke in Mara's voice: “The key goes to the youngest hand. The comb goes to the one who divided. The thread goes to the one who hears.”

Tovan heard his instruction and removed the comb from his grip. Eren took the spool from his pocket. Ivara placed the key on the chair. The chalk moth's wings folded again, and she took the key back into her hand. For one brief moment the paper wall showed the names without their crossed-out marks. Then the names faded, leaving only the grooves behind.

Nima was not there, but Ivara could hear the Orchard keeper somewhere above them, striking the branches with a washer. The three-note song traveled down through the floors. They followed it to the Understair, carrying the objects that had begun to choose their own bearers.

text:
After leaving the hidden chamber, Ivara went to the Hall's record shelves alone. She wanted to see the winter roll where Pell Aven had disappeared. The file began with a child's name and ended with a blank space. No death had been recorded, no transfer, no dismissal. The space was clean in the way a room looks after furniture has been removed.

She found a second copy of the roll stored under the old title “Names without a door.” This version had notes in Mara's hand. Pell's line read, “The porter is not missing; the Hall is asking the wrong question.” Beneath it, the name Eren Vey appeared with a mark for temporary residence in the first house. Mara had kept the evidence, but she had not given it to Tovan. Perhaps she believed that records could be both a shield and a trap.

Ivara took neither file. She memorized the note and closed the shelf. For the first time, she understood why her mother had left the red key with her rather than in the Hall's custody. A key could be used to open something, but it could also remind its bearer not to lock a room merely because it was difficult to explain.

When she returned to the Understair, Eren Vey was sitting on the bottom step. He had unwound the numbered spool and wrapped its thread around his fingers. He said he could hear two voices in it now: the voice of the room, and the voice of the person who had carried the spool there. He did not know which one had spoken his name.

“Does it matter?” she asked.

“It matters if I pretend one voice is the other.”

He rolled the spool closed and stood. He was not ready to tell them about the night he had spent in the first house, but he had stopped believing the song belonged only to his mother. Ivara did not press him. Her own memories had begun to feel like rooms she could enter at her own pace.

Above them, the Hall's clerks were changing shifts. Their steps moved across the ceiling in careful lines. The Understair caught each one and sent it down as a different sound: a heel became a tap, a pause became a hum, a hurried footfall became a door. The building was teaching them that a single journey could be recorded in several true ways.

text:
# Chapter 4: The Stair That Counted Down

The Nacre Stair descended through the shell of Oru. Its steps were made from polished pieces of something that might once have been a giant clam, though no one in the city agreed on whether clams had ever been alive. The stair counted backward from nine hundred each time someone crossed it. It was said that if the count reached zero, the steps would become a single flat floor.

Nima waited on step 412. The brass washers on her necklace clicked with each breath. She had left the Tin Orchard without permission, and her sleeves were dusted with pale grit. In her hands she carried a folded bark strip bearing the word LATCH.

“I thought you said the room was your grandmother's,” Ivara said.

“It was the only story the Orchard gave me.” Nima ran a thumb over the strip. “I found this below the empty ring. It has my grandmother's handwriting, but it says the room was made by four children.”

Tovan asked who the other children were.

“Ivara's sister. Pell. Me.” Nima looked at her. “And you.”

“I wasn't there.”

“You were the baby in the house. They wrote your name on the wall before you could speak.”

Nima had learned what the others did not: her grandmother did not build the Latch alone. The claim that the Latch belonged to her family was a lie inherited from an older lie, and she had come to correct it. She held the bark strip out to Ivara, who put it beside the brass map. The two records aligned, though neither showed an entrance.

The stair rang below them. The count changed from 412 to 411. Someone was climbing upward.

Eren Vey tied a loose end of black thread to the numbered spool without unspooling it from the glass thimble. The two threads twitched toward one another. “This line leads to the first house.”

Tovan seized the spool. “No. It leads to the split. If you pull it, the rooms will join, and everyone inside will be moved.”

“You knew that,” said Ivara. “You hid Alis there because you knew.”

“I hid the child because there was nowhere else that would hold her name.”

Pell watched Tovan's hands. “The seventh tooth can stop the comb. You once told me it was lost.”

“I told you it was dangerous.”

The red key warmed. Tovan had lied to Pell about the tooth being lost, even though he believed the danger was real.

Nima placed a washer on the step. The stair count paused. “The Orchard has a rule. A room can be claimed only by everyone who remembers entering it.”

“That's not a rule,” said Tovan. “That's a superstition.”

“Then it won't hurt to try.”

They set the brass map on the landing. Pell opened the tin box and took out its false bottom. Under the lifted false bottom, a depression in the box held nothing now but a dark outline shaped like a key. The objects they had brought were divided among them: map to Eren Vey, thimble to Ivara, comb to Tovan, and box to Pell. The empty outline was not an absence. It was a place waiting for the red key.

Ivara set the key into the depression. The stair gave a low note and stopped counting. A rectangular outline appeared in the shell wall, then another, then another. On the lowest step, someone had scratched “ALIS NOLL” in a child's hand.

Ivara's remembered claim changed: Alis had not been buried in the family niche. She had been hidden alive in the first house. That fact now belonged to all four of them, but Eren Vey knew an additional thing. He had heard the name at the end of the spool: it was his own. As a child, he had been placed in the first house too, for a single night, and his mother took him away before the split. He had kept this from the others because he feared the Registry would decide he belonged to a room instead of himself.

He unwound the spool. His name made the black thread draw taut. The wall opened at the level of the landing, not below, and beyond it was a room with a child-sized chair, a chalk moth, and the sound of someone turning pages.

“Alis?” called Ivara.

A woman's voice answered, “Still here.”

text:
The stair resumed its count, but now it counted upward. Nima's washers chimed. Tovan reached for the bone comb, and Pell blocked him.

“You can't make the first house hold by combing it into pieces,” Pell said. “We have to bring it back together.”

Tovan looked at the opening. “If you join it, the Hall loses its boundaries.”

“The Hall is a room,” said Ivara. “It can learn to share.”

She lifted the key from the depression in the box and gave it to Nima. Nima held the key and the bark strip. The red iron stayed cool against her palm; she had spoken truth. She had not come to claim the room. She had come to return it.

The four children named in the old record were now grown, and not all were present. Still, Ivara stepped through first.

Before they entered the opening, Ivara asked Nima why she had trusted the old story for so long. Nima told her that in the Orchard, every child received a washer from the keeper and was told the tree it came from. Her grandmother's washer had been smooth with use. When Nima was young, she had asked whether the Latch had belonged to their family. Her grandmother had answered, “It was ours to protect.” Nima had mistaken the words for “ours to own.”

The difference had shaped her whole life. She became keeper because she thought she had inherited a duty that belonged to her bloodline. Now she had learned that protection was temporary and ownership was not the same thing as care. She took the necklace from her throat and placed it on the landing. Each washer rang once, as if relieved to be off duty.

The memory of Mara Noll came to Ivara in scraps. Her mother had never said that Alis was dead; she had said Alis was “in the niche,” the phrase used in Oru for a place where a family keeps what it cannot carry. Ivara had read “in the niche” as “buried” because the Hall's register had used the word unplaced. There had been a mistake, then a correction, then another mistake built on top of it.

The stair carried them upward by degrees. A person could cross the same step twice and arrive at a different landing. Pell marked their route with small folds of paper. Eren Vey laid the black thread along the handrail. Tovan followed behind with no tool in his hand, as if he were trying to learn what a room sounded like without the comb.

At one landing, the stair opened onto the Tin Orchard. The rust-colored branches crowded the threshold. Nima recognized the empty tray where the Latch's hinge had lain. She placed the red key in the grit and waited. The ground did not open, but a nearby tree bent its roots around the metal. The key's forked tooth matched the shape of the hinge pin. It had never been a door key in the ordinary sense; it was a memory of the hinge that joined the Orchard to the first house.

Nima lifted it out. “My grandmother didn't make the room. She kept one side from falling away.”

That was the correction she would carry back to the Orchard. Her grandmother had not been the sole maker of the Latch, but she had done something important. The old story was not entirely false. It had simply made one person stand where four belonged.

They went on. When they reached the opening, Ivara saw the room's five places set for them. She realized that the table was not waiting for five people who had all lived there. It was waiting for five people who could remember it differently. The house had no use for matching memories. It needed a place where the disagreements could remain visible.

Eren Vey stopped before the threshold. His private memory of one night in the house had given him a claim, but he feared that speaking it would make the room keep him. He asked Ivara to listen to the spool for him. She refused gently. “It belongs in your hearing.”

He placed the thread against his ear and stepped over the threshold. The room took a breath. The door behind him did not close.

text:
When Nima returned the washer necklace to the Orchard, she did not put it back around her throat. She tied it to the hinge in the empty tray. The metal pieces hung there like a small, uneven curtain. Each washer had once marked a year of her own life; now it marked a year in which the Orchard had cared for something without claiming it.

The other keepers asked what she meant by saying her grandmother had not made the Latch. Nima repeated the four-child story and showed them the strip. Some were relieved. They had never liked the tale of one grandmother building an impossible room alone. Others worried that if nobody owned the Latch, no one would be responsible when it moved.

Nima told them responsibility could be shared. She offered to keep the empty tray open and to report whenever the hinge sang. She would no longer say that the room belonged to her family. The Orchard accepted this modestly: one tree released a fruit, and another turned a leaf toward the stair.

Meanwhile, Ivara followed the thread through the wall and noticed that it did not pass through solid matter. It crossed the wall at a place where a person had once paused. The path was made from attention, not distance. Eren Vey understood this too. He let the spool trail behind him but did not wind it around his wrist. The line stretched only as far as he could continue listening.

Pell recognized a mark on the landing and told them it was one he had scratched as a child. He had made it to remember which direction led back to the first house. In the divided city, the same mark had been copied onto several doorways, and none of them led back. He rubbed it with his thumb. Beneath the old mark, the shell showed a new one: a loop with four smaller loops inside.

The stair was not restoring the way it had been. It was making a way that included their separate memories. The climb became easier once they stopped trying to match their steps. Tovan walked slowly. Nima went ahead. Eren listened at each landing. Ivara and Pell took turns holding the thread.

At the last threshold, they could all hear the same voice, though each of them would later describe it differently. The room had not asked them to agree. It had asked them to arrive.

text:
# Chapter 5: The Room With Four Names

The room beyond the Nacre Stair had a floor of soft gray felt. It was larger inside than the city could contain. A table stood in the middle, set for five. There were four chairs and one stool, each with a name marked beneath it. Ivara found ALIS on the chair by the wall. On the stool was her own name, written twice: once in her mother's hand, once in a hand she did not recognize.

Alis Noll sat at the table. She had not aged the way people in Oru aged. Her hair was short and white at the temples; her face held the tiredness of an adult who had once waited a very long time as a child. Eren Vey set the brass map before her, though its lines had become threads.

Ivara stopped a pace away. “I thought you were dead.”

“I was dead in the register,” said Alis. “That is not the same thing.”

The truth was plain, but it did not make the years less strange. Alis had stayed in the first house while the rooms divided around her. She could leave only when someone remembered the first house as one place. Those outside could hear her, but they could not agree on where she was. The Hall called its answering chamber the Mouth Room. The Orchard called the missing room the Latch. The Nacre Stair carried its count. These were connected rooms and ways of hearing the first house, not the same room.

Ivara put the glass thimble on the table. “This came from the box.”

Alis took the black thread from inside the thimble, unlooped it from the spool, and looped it around one finger. “Our mother hid a line here so the room would never forget the way back.”

Tovan entered last. He held the bone comb close to his chest. “I kept you safe.”

“You kept me still,” Alis replied. “You knew I was alive and let Ivara mourn me.”

“I thought the city would erase you if it knew.”

“Maybe. But you chose for everyone.”

Tovan's face seemed smaller in the large room. He set the comb on the table. The numbered teeth trembled. Eren Vey produced the spool from his coat. The seventh tooth came loose from its thread and fell beside the comb. Its thread had formed a small loop that fit around the comb's empty place.

The Hall's old examiner had spent years carrying the bone comb, pretending it belonged to a museum. He had been right to fear its power, but wrong to think that withholding it could preserve the first house. It had only made the fragments harder to find.

Nima laid down the bark strip with the four children's names. Beside each was a blank space. “The Orchard can remember the room if it has a keeper,” she said. “The Hall can remember it if it has an address. The stair can remember it if it has a count. None of us can keep it alone.”

Pell sat on the floor. “The Latch never needed a keeper. It needed people to stop calling it theirs.”

At that, the red key, still in Nima's hand, stayed cool. Pell's words were true.

Alis offered Eren Vey a place. He did not take it. “I was there once,” he said. “I don't know what else I can promise.”

“Nothing,” she said. “You can remember one night.”

He told them how his mother carried him through the first house, how every door opened before she touched it, and how the walls gave a low note when she sang. He had kept the memory private, thinking it would make the room claim him. Instead, the lines on the brass map joined into a single loop. Ivara folded the map and kept it.

A door opened in the wall. Beyond it was the Sump, with its clay floor and stone basin. The Understair lay beyond the Sump. The room could now reach the Hall, the Orchard, and the stair. It had become a place again, though not one with a single address.

Ivara asked Alis why she had not called sooner.

“I did. You were too young to know the sound was a name.”

text:
The explanation landed gently. Ivara remembered a lullaby from childhood, a note that made her mother stop sewing and press her hand against the wall. That was when the red key first appeared in her mother's apron. Ivara had carried the key ever since, believing it to be an unclaimed tool. She had not known that it was her mother's promise to come back.

Tovan told Alis he was sorry. She did not forgive him, and she did not send him away. She asked him to carry the comb to the Mouth Room and let it hear the true name of the chamber. He accepted the work without asking for absolution.

Pell gave the tin box to Alis. She turned it over and found a mark on the underside: four small loops and one larger one. The box had been made to store the first house's five names, not its walls. The false bottom had carried the map, thread, thimble, and message; its emptiness had kept a space for the key.

Outside the wall, the Nacre Stair counted 1, 2, 3. It had stopped counting down. The old count had never measured steps. It measured how many names remained before the room was divided beyond repair.

Alis rose from the table. “Let's go tell the Hall it has a neighbor.”

Alis showed them how the first house had survived. When the Hall and Orchard were split, the room's walls did not break. The door that had scarred Eren Vey had not belonged to a vanished wall, as he had believed; it was one of the first house's thresholds, folded away when the room divided. Instead, each fragment received one of its names. The Latch was the name Nima heard at the Orchard. First House was what Mara called it. The child-sized chamber beneath the Understair was its memory of being small. The Mouth Room remained a separate answering chamber, connected to the first house by a shared wall. The fragments remembered the first house, but were not all the same room.

Mara had copied the ancient room plan onto the brass map from memory. She had made it small enough to fold into the box, thinking that a map could preserve a way home. But the map showed the names, not the walls, because walls could move. The black thread was a route held by a person rather than a line. Every time someone remembered a way into the first house, the thread gained another strand.

Alis had never heard the full story about her own arrival. Mara brought her through the Mouth Room as a baby, after finding her alone in a room that had lost its address. The Hall treated her as an unplaced child and prepared to assign her a place in the registry. Mara refused. She said the child had already been found by a room that could hold her. The first house called her Alis Noll and accepted the name.

“I don't know who gave me the name before that,” Alis said. “Maybe no one. Maybe the room did.”

The account changed the way Ivara understood her sister. Alis had not been taken from her family by the Partition. She had been brought into it, and then the Partition hid the room that had welcomed her. The Hall's record was accurate about Alis being unplaced at birth, but wrong to treat that as a defect to be corrected.

Tovan listened without interruption. When Alis finished, he confessed that he had written “buried in the niche” on the old ledger because he could not bear to leave the line blank. He thought a completed form would protect Ivara from a question she was too young to ask. Instead, his neat writing gave her a false memory.

Alis let him finish. “You may carry the comb,” she said. “You may not decide what it does.”

He nodded. That was not forgiveness, but it was a boundary he understood.

text:
Pell found a drawer beneath the table. Inside was a paper bird folded from a strip of an old address. He knew the handwriting: his own, from when he was a child. On its wing he had written “Pell Aven.” He gave the bird to Eren Vell, who read the name and then tucked it into his coat. For years, Pell had believed the porter name was the only one the Hall would let him keep. Now he had the old name as well, not as a replacement but as a piece of his history.

Nima asked whether the Latch would return to the Orchard. Alis said it could visit, but it would not be stored inside a tree again. A room that belonged to several people could not be put away in one person's container. Nima agreed. She would leave the empty tray open, with the hinge visible, so visitors could see where the joining had been.

The table shook once. The four chairs and the stool shifted to face the open door. The first house had finished remembering its way back.

The room kept its own time. They ate nothing, slept not at all, yet each felt the afternoon pass as surely as if a bell had marked it. Alis said the first house did not measure hours. It measured visits. Whenever someone came in, the room made room for that person's memory. When someone left, it kept the shape of the memory without keeping the person.

Ivara asked whether Alis had been lonely. Alis said yes, and no. For a long time, she had been the only person who could enter. Then, whenever the Hall asked a question through the Mouth Room, she could hear it. Whenever Nima passed the empty tray, Alis could hear the washer. She had been surrounded by people who did not know how close they were.

“That's a peculiar kind of company,” Ivara said.

“It is. I don't recommend it.”

They laughed. The room responded by shifting the table a little closer to the door. The movement felt less like magic than courtesy.

Alis showed Ivara a mark under the stool, made by a child with a blunt tool. It was a crooked line that looked like a road. Ivara remembered drawing it in the bark dust while Mara read aloud. She had no memory of the room itself, only the warmth beneath the drawer where she slept. The mark gave the warmth a shape.

Pell told them what he remembered of the four children: Nima had insisted every room needed a name; Alis wanted no name that could be used as a lock; he had argued for a door that could be folded away; and Ivara, too small to join the argument, had chosen the place where all their voices could be heard. The story made Ivara feel as though she had helped build the house, even if she could not remember doing it.

Tovan asked Alis whether the room would hold him now. She said it already did, but that was not the same as excusing what he had done. He accepted the distinction. He sat at the fifth place and listened while the others spoke about the years between then and now. No one made him the center of the story, but no one pushed him outside it.

By the time the map's lines had settled, they could see the route each person had taken to reach the table. The routes were different. All of them led to a seat.

text:
# Chapter 6: A Neighboring Address

They returned by the Nacre Stair, which now climbed without counting. The Tin Orchard opened its gate as they approached. The metal leaves stopped clicking and held still, listening. Nima went ahead to tell the trees that the Latch had never belonged to her grandmother alone. She spoke the corrected story without apology. Some of the trees rang in agreement; others stayed quiet. An Orchard could be stubborn without being cruel.

At the Vellum Hall, Tovan carried the bone comb into the Mouth Room. He asked it to say the true name. The black circular door opened, and the chamber inside sounded not like a spoon touching a cup, but like five spoons laid carefully on a table.

“First House,” Ivara said.

The room answered by opening a second door. Through it, they saw Alis standing in the Latch, with the tin box on the stool Alis had used in the first house. Nima still held the red key. From that day, the Hall and the first house shared a wall. Clerks could visit the room, but they had to ask before recording anything inside it.

The decision upset the Registry. A room without a single registered address was, to the clerks, an argument rather than a place. Tovan stood before the Hall's assembly and admitted that he had known Alis was alive. He also admitted that he had hidden the seventh tooth, and that his claim that the Latch could not open again was false. He did not claim that fear excused him. He asked to remain examiner until someone else could hear rooms as well as he could.

The assembly gave him one day a week, and assigned the other six to Eren Vey. The two Eren’s signed the same sheet. Eren Vell kept the name he had chosen after the Hall erased Pell Aven. On the reverse side of the form, he wrote “Pell Aven” so the old name would not vanish. Both names were his; neither was the Hall's property.

Ivara asked Alis what the red key opened. Alis placed it on the table.

“Nothing,” Alis said. “It reminds a door that it can choose.”

Nima handed the key to Alis. It had been Mara's, then Ivara's, and now it belonged to the person who had waited longest for it. Alis placed it in the tin box, whose false bottom folded down to make an ordinary bottom at last. The brass map stayed with Ivara, the glass thimble returned to the Mouth Room, and the numbered spool went to Eren Vey. The bone comb remained with Tovan. Each object had a new place, though no ledger agreed about which place mattered most.

The chalk moth stayed in the hidden chamber beneath the Understair. Once a month, Pell visited it and told it one thing that had changed. He never tried to remove it. The moth had become the chamber's small guardian, flat enough to fit in a book and stubborn enough to hold a name.

Nima continued keeping the Tin Orchard, but she stopped wearing one washer for each year. She untied the washers from the hinge and threaded them onto a cord around a young tree instead. If someone asked whether her grandmother had made the Latch, Nima said, “She helped remember it.” The answer did not satisfy everyone. It was accurate.

Alis came to the Hall on the first day of every new cycle. She sat in the Mouth Room and let the clerks ask their questions. Sometimes she answered. Sometimes the chamber answered first. Neither one was mistaken for the other anymore.

Ivara kept her desk beside the shared wall. A new strip of bark lay there, blank except for a line that read: “A room may have more than one address.” She had not written it. The bark had grown that sentence from a pressure in the wall.

One evening, while the Hall was closing, Eren Vey heard a soft note come from beneath Ivara's desk. He placed the numbered spool on the floor and let it turn. It rolled toward the wall and stopped at a crack no wider than a hair.

The first house had begun to hum.

Ivara did not take out the key. She did not call the examiner. She knelt and listened. On the other side, a child laughed, then someone older laughed with them. The sounds belonged to different people, though they shared a room.

text:
The Vellum Hall's map acquired a second loop. No clerk tried to cut it away. By morning, the map had moved the Hall's desk, the Orchard's hinge, and the stair's first step a little closer together. The city of Oru remained where it had always been, if “where” could still be said of a place that listened.

The blank address strip filled itself with five names: Alis Noll, Ivara Noll, Pell Aven, Nima Orrel, and Eren Vey. Beneath them, in a smaller hand, appeared Eren Vell. The porter looked at the strip and smiled at the clerk. “Both,” he said, when Ivara asked which name should go on the file.

She left the strip unpinned after that. Some things were easier to find when no one tried to own their names.

There were practical matters after the ceremony. The Hall's clerks needed a way to write an address for a room that had several doors and no fixed boundary. Ivara proposed that they list the names people used, then leave a space for any name the room might choose later. The senior clerks objected that an empty line could not be audited. Eren Vey pointed out that the old records had contained full names and still lost an entire person.

Tovan sat beside the map and said nothing. When asked, he offered no defense of the old system. He said he could teach the younger clerks to listen before they wrote. His examiner's chair was moved beside the shared wall, so that he could hear both the Hall and the first house. The Chair no longer had to remain seated to make a decision; he chose the new place himself.

Nima returned to the Orchard for a single afternoon. She left the empty tray open and told the trees that the red key had passed through their hands. The trees kept the impression of the iron in the grit. That was enough.

Pell visited the Hall's record room and asked for the winter roll where Pell Aven had disappeared. The clerk who brought it out could not find a line for him. Pell wrote his own name in the margin and signed Eren Vell beneath it. The two names sat next to each other without an arrow between them. A new clerk asked whether that meant they were two people. Pell answered, “It means I am here twice in the book.”

The clerk left the entry as it was.

Eren Vey continued to hear the spool's quiet song. He used it to find rooms that had been pushed behind walls or folded into stairs, but he never pulled the thread without asking who else could hear it. Sometimes it led to an empty cupboard. Sometimes it led to a room whose occupant had forgotten they were allowed to open the door. He brought no rooms to the Hall by force.

Ivara found a drawer in her desk that had not been there before. It contained the shell-milk recipe sheet she had searched for, in Mara Noll's handwriting. The recipe was for shell milk, but beneath the ingredients Mara had written a note on the recipe sheet: “If Alis comes home by a different door, let her choose which one is hers.” Ivara kept the sheet beside the blank address strip. Her mother had known the return might happen, though she had not known when or how.

When Ivara asked Alis what she wanted the Hall to call her, Alis answered “Alis” and nothing more. The register printed “Alis Noll” because that was the name the room had kept for her. No one wrote “unplaced.”

On the next cycle's first day, the five names on the strip rearranged themselves. The order changed, but each remained legible. The clerk responsible for the map tried to pin the strip down. The pin bent. Ivara told him to let it move. He looked uncomfortable, then tucked the pin back into his sleeve.

That evening, the Hall doors stayed open late. People came from the Orchard and the lower stair to hear the shared wall hum. Some brought old names; others brought no names at all. The room did not answer everyone. It did not have to. Being heard was not the price of being allowed to enter.

text:
When the lamps dimmed, Ivara went to the Mouth Room. She asked if it wanted an official address. The chamber answered with five soft notes, then a pause for a sixth. Ivara waited. A sixth note came from the other side of the wall, not from the room but from a person walking home.

The Hall altered its forms slowly. First it added a box for “other names.” Then it added a line for “room's chosen address.” The oldest clerks insisted that these were temporary measures. The youngest clerks filled the boxes with names they had never been allowed to record before. One wrote down the name a stair used for itself. Another entered a room that was known only by the sound of someone laughing in it.

Ivara reviewed the changes, not as a new examiner but as a clerk who knew what it felt like to see a familiar name on an unfamiliar line. She returned the forms that treated a person as a room's possession. She accepted the forms that recorded who had chosen an address and who had chosen to leave it blank.

Tovan trained himself to listen with both ears. The comb stayed on his desk, but he stopped using it to divide a room's notes. He taught that a sound could have several sources and still be one sound. Some trainees found this difficult. He let them struggle, as he had once refused to let others do.

Nima came to the Hall with a small metal fruit from the Orchard. It contained no address. She opened it anyway. Inside was only a pale ring of grit, the outline left by the Latch's old hinge. She set the fruit beside the map. Ivara wrote no label on it. They let it sit without deciding what it meant.

Eren Vell kept the paper bird in his coat. The porter still carried bark strips from one desk to another, but now he could choose which name to give when someone asked who he was. Sometimes he said Eren Vell. Sometimes he wrote Pell Aven. When someone called Eren, both men still looked up, and the younger clerks still laughed. The joke no longer cost anyone a minute of pay.

Alis never moved into a single room. She lived where she chose from day to day, sometimes in the Hall, sometimes in the first house, and sometimes among the trees. No ledger followed her unless she invited it. She was not a mystery the city had solved. She was a person whose life had become visible again.

The last sound Ivara heard before the Hall closed was the shared wall giving its six notes. She could name five of them. The sixth belonged to whoever was coming home. The Hall did not ask for that person's name before opening the door.
